Tipping the scales in Blue Jay: Dust energy balance overpredicts IR luminosity in galaxies at $z\sim2$

Benjamin P. Collins, Sirio Belli, Letizia Bugiani, Amir H. Khoram, Minjung Park +7

18 pages, 15 figures, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics

PDFThu 26 Nov
The spectral energy distribution (SED) of a galaxy encodes vital information about its chemical composition, stellar populations, and dust content. To model the infrared emission, many modern SED-fitting codes rely on dust energy balance, which assumes that all energy absorbed by dust in the UV-optical is equal to the energy emitted by dust in the infrared regime. However, few studies have been carried out to test the validity of this assumption at high redshift, where direct infrared observations are sparse. In this work, we perform aperture photometry in 111 galaxies from the Blue Jay survey ($1.7 < z < 3.5$) using public JWST/MIRI observations from the PRIMER, COSMOS-Web and COSMOS-3D surveys. Focusing on a subsample of 89 star-forming galaxies, we reconstruct best-fit SED model spectra from Prospector using only HST and NIRCam photometry and compare the predicted mid-infrared fluxes to the measured MIRI photometry. We find that mid-infrared fluxes are systematically overpredicted by about 10% at 7.7$\mu$m up to a factor of $\sim3$ at 21$\mu$m. The discrepancy increases with inferred dust attenuation, indicating that dust energy balance suffers from line-of-sight effects in systems with complex dust geometries. We find that adding NIRSpec spectroscopy to the fits breaks parameter degeneracies and strongly reduces the overprediction. When fitting the measured MIRI photometry together with the HST and NIRCam data, the best-fit model spectra of dusty galaxies ($A_V\gtrsim1$) result in significantly lower infrared luminosities by -0.6 dex compared to best-fit spectra obtained without MIRI, consistent with steeper, SMC-like attenuation curves or complex star-dust geometries. Our study highlights the limitations of dust energy balance at high redshift and underlines the importance of direct observations for accurately recovering the ISM and dust properties of galaxies at cosmic noon.

State of the UNIONS: Four Milky Way companions discovered in a systematic search for northern Local Group satellites

Simon E. T. Smith, Alan W. McConnachie, Thomas de Boer, Ken C. Chambers, Stephen Gwyn +6

27 pages, 7 figures in main text, 4 figures in appendix; Accepted for publication in ApJ

PDFThu 26 Nov
We present four newly discovered Milky Way satellites from a systematic search through the $gri$ photometry from the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS). Two of these satellites are likely ultra-faint dwarf galaxies that we have named Boötes VI and Draco III. Both galaxy candidates are $\gtrsim 100$ kpc from the Galactic center and have absolute $V$-band magnitudes ($M_V$) of $-2.7^{+0.6}_{-0.5}$ and $-4.0\pm0.6$, respectively. Boötes VI and Draco III have physical half-light radii ($r_{\rm h}$) of $\sim 50$ pc, or about twice as large as the most extended Milky Way globular clusters with similar luminosities. They are therefore candidate galaxies, though chemodynamical analyses will be needed to secure these classifications. We name the two other systems UNIONS 2 and UNIONS 3. They are extremely faint ($M_V = +0.4^{+0.6}_{-0.9}$ and $-0.7^{+0.6}_{-0.8}$) and compact ($r_{\rm h} = 5\,\pm\,1$ and $10^+3_-2 pc), and zero giant stars are identified in either of their present-day stellar populations. Morphological measurements alone are not sufficient to assess the presence of dark matter in either system, so do not provide definitive classifications. We discuss the challenges in either detecting or refuting the presence of dark matter in UNIONS 2 and UNIONS 3, two systems that are archetypal of the faintest satellites that will be discovered in increasing numbers in upcoming wide-field surveys.

RR Lyrae stars as distance indicators I. Sample selection and characterisation

M. Sánchez-Benavente, M. Monelli, M. Dall'Ora, V. F. Braga, J. P. Mullen +11

Paper accepted for publication in the section "7. Stellar structure and evolution" of Astronomy & Astrophysics. 20 pages, 11 figures, 10 tables

PDFThu 26 Nov
RR Lyrae stars (RRL) are well-established Population II distance indicators, with period-metallicity-luminosity (PLZ) relations linking pulsational properties to absolute luminosity. Gaia parallaxes now allow these relations to be anchored to geometric distances with unprecedented precision, offering an independent route to the extragalactic distance scale. We present the first paper in a series aimed at deriving new empirical PLZ and metallicity-luminosity relations for RRL in the optical and near-infrared. We describe the selection and characterisation of a sample of bright nearby field RRL, with distances anchored to reliable Gaia DR3 parallaxes. We conducted a multi-band photometric campaign of 172 RRL: 101 in Johnson-Cousins UBVRI with the IAC80 telescope and 130 in JHKs with the IRSF telescope, with 59 stars in common. The iron abundances come from the Spectroscopic Rome RRL Catalog catalogue, mostly from high-resolution spectroscopy. The light curves were modelled with GLOESS (optical) and near-infrared templates, and the mean magnitudes, amplitudes, and Fourier parameters were derived via a bootstrap Monte Carlo method. The linear relations were fitted with a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo method. The sample spans -3.4 to 0.2 dex in [Fe/H]. We found tight relations between the Fourier parameter $\phi_{31}$ in each optical and Gaia band and its V-band value for RRab stars (scatter below 0.06). The near-infrared amplitude ratios with respect to V or G increase continuously with period, without the break reported in globular clusters. We provide a homogeneous calibration of the colour at minimum light across all filter combinations from U-B to H-Ks, revealing significant period and metallicity dependences, and we use it to derive reddening estimates for 15 stars outside current 3D extinction maps.

The Splash population confined to the Milky Way bar region

Aakash Pandey, Ortwin Gerhard

19 pages, 12 main article figures, 3 appendix figures, submitted to MNRAS

PDFThu 26 Nov
We investigate the chemo-dynamical properties of in-situ stars in the Galactic bar region (central $5$ kpc), specifically the inner Galactic counterpart of the solar-neighbourhood Splash population (in situ halo). We use a sample of APOGEE DR17 red giants with Gaia astrometry and AstroNN distances, and separate bulge/bar stellar populations dynamically using a normalised time-averaged bar-frame angular momentum, $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}$. Chemo-dynamical maps in the $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}$-[Fe/H] plane reveal a pronounced extension of the bar population towards $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}<0$ (non-bar-following orbits) within $-1.0<{\rm [Fe/H]}<-0.3$, characterised by high eccentricities, large $z_{\rm max}$ and an extended spheroidal orbit density distribution, and accounting for $\sim 30\%$ of all stars at these metallicities. These $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}<0$ stars have [Mg/Fe] and [Al/Fe] abundances similar to those of stars on ${\rm x_1}$ orbits at the same [Fe/H], and they match the solar-neighbourhood Splash in its metallicity and abundance ratio distributions. We therefore refer to them as the $\textit{central Splash}$. The presence of a significant central Splash underscores the role of the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger in the early history of the Galaxy. We find a similar, weaker extension in the $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}$-[Fe/H] maps for extremely metal-rich stars, which are confined to the bulge. At metallicities [Fe/H] $<0.3$, we find no additional classical bulge population in these maps beyond the central Splash and proto-Galactic populations $-$ the high-$\alpha$ bulge appears to have evolved from the early high-$\alpha$ disc.

UNIONS and Euclid: Calibrating point source-galaxy separation for ground-based surveys

G. Thomas, S. E. T. Smith, S. Gwyn, A. W. McConnachie, J.-C. Cuillandre +95

Accepted for publication in A&A. Some material is available online on this https URL

PDFThu 26 Nov
Efficient separation of unresolved point sources from extended objects (star-galaxy separation) is essential for deep wide-field imaging surveys, particularly at faint magnitudes where morphological differences become subtle. We assess two morphology-based classification methods applied to single-band, ground-based imaging from the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS), using Euclid observations as a high-fidelity reference to evaluate their performance and to train one of the methods. We analysed 8 deg$^2$ of overlapping UNIONS $r$-band and Euclid $I_E$ data, comprising more than $7\times10^{5}$ sources. The Euclid data enable robust morphological labelling down to $I_E\simeq 26$, which we used to train and validate two classification approaches applied to UNIONS alone: a curve-of-growth method and a supervised neural-network classifier, both based on aperture photometry and image-quality information. The curve-of-growth method yields an almost perfectly complete point-source sample ($>95\%$), but its purity decreases rapidly at $r \simeq 22.5$. The neural-network approach significantly improves the purity at the faint end, maintaining $\geq 80\%$ purity down to $r \simeq 24$, while the completeness decreases to almost $50\%$ at similar depths. In both cases, performance strongly depends on the image quality of the ground-based data. This work shows how Euclid data can be used to develop, calibrate, and validate star-galaxy separation methods for ground-based surveys, useful in regions not covered by Euclid. Both methods have already been applied to UNIONS data and are readily applicable to future surveys such as LSST, offering flexible solutions depending on whether completeness or purity is prioritised.

Towards three-dimensional dark matter mapping in the extended solar neighbourhood with Gaia Data Release 3 and deep learning

Yigon Kim, Ho Seong Hwang, Sungwook E. Hong, Donghui Jeong, Mingyeong Yang +1

17 pages, 15 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS on the Nov. 24, 2026

PDFThu 26 Nov
We investigate a method for inferring the local dark matter (DM) density in the solar neighbourhood using a deep learning framework that learns the mapping between stellar kinematics and the underlying DM density field from cosmological simulations. To this end, we construct a training set from 7 Milky Way-like galaxies in the FIRE-2 simulation suite. We use three-dimensional stellar kinematic components, consisting of the tangential velocities along the right ascension and declination directions ($v_{\alpha*}$ and $v_{\delta}$) derived from parallaxes and proper motions, together with radial velocity, as input features to predict the three-dimensional DM density field. Two distinct architectures, VNet (arXiv:1606.04797) and ViT-VNet (arXiv:2205.08534), are trained on identical datasets. Both models reproduce the large-scale DM density gradient, whereas small-scale fluctuations are systematically smoothed. Applying the trained models to Gaia DR3 data yields our best estimates of the local DM density: $0.80^{+0.10}_{-0.10}$ and $1.12^{+0.15}_{-0.13}$ GeV cm$^{-3}$ from VNet and ViT-VNet, respectively. The quoted uncertainties reflect the inference scatter across the training set. We further examine systematics from model dependence and the simulation-Gaia domain mismatch, providing an initial step towards a framework for reconstructing local DM maps from future multi-epoch astrometric measurements, including those expected from Gaia DR4.

The THESAN-ZOOM project: interpreting candidate Population III-enriched absorption line systems during reionization

Giulia Pruto, Laura Keating, Rahul Kannan, Ewald Puchwein, Aaron Smith +5

23 pages, 15 figures, submitted to MNRAS

PDFThu 26 Nov
With JWST, metal absorption lines are now being detected at increasingly high redshift, where signatures of the first generation of stars (Population III) may be observable. Interpreting observations of possible Pop III-enriched gas is challenging, as metals released by stars inevitably mix with pristine gas accreting onto galaxies and recycled gas from different episodes of star formation. Inference of Pop III enrichment from low-ionisation absorption lines requires placing stellar nucleosynthesis yields within the broader context of galaxy evolution. With THESAN-ZOOM, a set of high-resolution radiation hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations of galaxies, we investigate the metal abundance patterns observable in absorption. As our fiducial simulations do not include Pop III enrichment channels, our primary goal is to test how galaxy formation processes can shape observed abundance ratios. Our results indicate that a single abundance ratio plane, such as the commonly used [Si/O] vs. [C/O], cannot conclusively distinguish Pop III enrichment from enrichment by subsequent populations of stars. Robust detections instead require characterising multiple abundance ratios. In our simulations, a larger dispersion in abundance ratio distributions (often interpreted as possible evidence of pollution from the first stellar populations) naturally arises with increasing redshift, when the metallicity and dust content are lower. However, this alone does not reproduce all the observed results. By running an additional simulation with an updated THESAN-ZOOM model containing Pop III stars, we show that this has a large impact on the simulated abundance ratios, pushing them closer to those observed in potential Pop III-enriched gas.

A Bayesian Approach to Prioritizing the Follow-Up of Near-Earth Objects

Devanshi Singh, Mario Jurić, Željko Ivezić

To be submitted to AAS Journals

PDFThu 26 Nov
We present pneo, a Bayesian classifier that computes the probability that a single-night tracklet belongs to a near-Earth object (NEO), using only its sky position, angular motion, and apparent magnitude. A tracklet does not determine the object's distance or radial velocity, so pneo integrates a model of the Solar System's small-body populations over all bound orbits consistent with it. The result is the exact posterior probability under that model, with no tuned scores or separately chosen priors: its classifications are optimal for the adopted model, and its probabilities are calibrated. On real discovery tracklets from the NEO Confirmation Page, the classifier is well calibrated and its selection is 1.14 times purer than that of digest2, the classifier now in use, at the same completeness. The advantage grows at Rubin's depth, where the faint background of main-belt and more distant objects is still largely undiscovered. On simulated tracklets to that depth, its selection is 2 times purer than that of digest2 (96% against 48%). On the Rubin alert stream and Rubin Data Preview 2 its selection is 1.4-1.7 times purer than that of digest2, and its predicted NEO counts are close to those observed. By raising the fraction of follow-up targets that are NEOs, pneo could potentially double the effective capacity of NEO follow-up in the Rubin era.

periapsis: A Comprehensive Orbital Fitting Package

Evan Kerr, Matthew Whitaker, Anil Seth, Jay Strader, Maximilian Häberle +1

14 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, submitted to MNRAS. Code available at this https URL. Comments welcome

PDFThu 26 Nov
We introduce a new Python package periapsis, which computes posterior distributions for a variety of orbital parameters given astrometric and/or radial velocity data. periapsis not only returns posterior distributions, but also a variety of statistics assessing convergence and fit metrics as well as plotting capabilities for visualizing the orbital systems. In this paper, we describe our various methods for fitting Keplerian orbits to both astrometric and radial velocity data. We then show the breadth of binary systems that periapsis can characterize by comparing our computed parameters with known orbital systems. Finally, we discuss how periapsis will be a helpful tool for future data releases like Gaia DR4 and Roman.

One, two, three, and a tilting frisbee: a transient state of some Be stars

Dietrich Baade, Jonathan Labadie-Bartz, Thomas Rivinius

16 pages. Accepted (after review) for publication in Proceedings of 42nd Liège Astrophysical Colloquium (LIAC42)

PDFThu 26 Nov
A recent reanalysis of the extreme variability of γ Cas in the 1930s/40s and 59 Cyg in the 1970s concluded that the disks of these two Be stars have each made a full turn over the poles (Baade+ 2023). For a better understanding of the underlying physics, more examples need to be identified, including less spectacular events, in which the disk was just tilted or warped. This paper discusses PZ Gem and HD 120678 as additional stars with spectroscopic evidence of a tilting disk: during extended line-emission periods intermittent shell phases occurred. In V1294 Aql, the symptoms of a tilting disk concerned Hα only. Three stars displayed heartbeat-like light variations. Unlike the original heartbeats resulting from distortions of red giant stars on an eccentric orbit, the much-larger-amplitude heartbeats in Be stars are due to changing orientations of the circumstellar disk. Two stars, Pleione and HD 120678, have exhibited both symptoms so that there is probably just one population of Be stars with tilting disks. The small number of candidates suggests that large-amplitude tilts/warpings of Be disks are not common. There is an extreme dominance of spectral types of B1 or earlier. In Be binaries resulting from previous mass transfer, spin-orbit misalignments and any torque on the Be disk should not be large. The necessary tilting force could be provided by a putative third star on an orbit highly inclined with respect to the inner binary (or just passing the B star) and be exerted either directly or indirectly via tilting the inner orbital plane. Beyond a refined knowledge of the multiplicity of Be stars, this would not promise much new insight into Be stars at large (except, perhaps, for some independent estimates of the viscosity parameter and a more 3D view of stellar winds). However, pruning the Be-star saga of such peculiarities may help reduce the level of confusion.

Less massive black holes in faint hosts: SED fitting of Little Red Dots within the Black Hole Star scenario

Haitong Liu, Lulu Fan, Yunkun Han, Yibin Luo

21 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal

PDFThu 26 Nov
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of compact sources known as “little red dots” (LRDs), characterized by a distinctive V-shaped spectral energy distribution (SED) from UV to optical wavelengths. The physical nature of these sources remains debated. The “black hole star” (BH*) scenario, wherein a super-Eddington accreting black hole is embedded in a dense gaseous envelope, has been proposed to explain them. We assemble a sample of 22 LRDs at $4.0 \lesssim z \lesssim 9.5$ from the ASTRODEEP-JWST database. We construct a composite “host galaxy + BH*” model using the Cloudy photoionization code, and perform SED fitting with BayeSED3. Our modeling reproduces the observed V-shaped features: the UV continuum blueward of the Balmer break is well reproduced by stellar emission within this decomposition, while the optical regime is dominated by the BH* component. Our fits reveal that LRDs are black holes hosted by faint, low-mass galaxies with median stellar and black hole masses of $M_* = 10^{8.7}\,M_\odot$ and $M_{\rm BH} = 10^{6.4}\,M_\odot$, respectively. These black holes are moderately overmassive relative to local scaling relations but less extreme than broad-line estimates. The median bolometric luminosity $L_{\rm BH^*} \sim 10^{44.9}\,\rm erg\,s^{-1}$ mitigates the reported number density tension from 1–2 orders of magnitude to a factor of a few. The host galaxies lie near the high-redshift star-forming main sequence, and stellar extinction correlates positively with star formation rate (SFR). The BH* scenario provides a self-consistent paradigm for LRDs, offering insights into the rapid growth of supermassive black hole seeds and their co-evolution with host galaxies during the cosmic dawn.

The tangled warp of the Milky Way II: The red clump

James E. Turner, Paul J. McMillan

10 pages, MNRAS submitted

PDFThu 26 Nov
The Milky Way's disc is warped in a way that varies depending on the age of the population considered. We, for the first time, trace that kinematics of the warp in red clumps stars. This means that our sample is drawn from a consistent population across the disc, composed of standard candles that allow for precise distance estimates but, unlike samples of Cepheid variables, is relatively old. We find that, consistent with other populations, the red-clump warp is precessing at ${\sim}12\;{\rm km}\,{\rm s}^{-1}\,{\rm kpc}^{-1}$, comparable to the angular velocity of stars around the Galaxy in the outer reaches of the disc. Unlike younger populations, the kinematic signature is offset from that which we would expect given the stellar positions. This reinforces the conclusion that the Milky Way's warp is dynamically evolving, making this a necessary property of any model that seeks to explain its creation.

Binary mass transfer fossil in the ancient GD-1 stellar stream

Guochao Yang, Sofya Alexeeva, Jingkun Zhao, Wako Aoki, Tatyana Sitnova +4

15 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJL

PDFThu 26 Nov
We report the discovery of J0930+2902, the first carbon-enhanced metal-poor star with s-process enrichment (CEMP-s) identified in the GD-1 stellar stream, which is widely believed to originate from the tidal disruption of an old, metal-poor globular cluster. Using high-resolution Subaru/HDS spectroscopy, we present a comprehensive chemical abundance analysis of this star. Stellar atmospheric parameters were re-derived using Gaia photometry and parallaxes, combined with an iterative non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) analysis of Fe lines. We determine abundances for 22 elements, including NLTE analyses of C, Na, Mg, Ca, Ti, Cr, Mn, Co, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, and Eu. J0930+2902 exhibits pronounced enhancements of C, N, Na, and s-process elements, together with a low $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio of 7.4, consistent with enrichment through binary mass transfer from a former asymptotic giant branch (AGB) companion. Large radial-velocity variations and a significant near-ultraviolet excess independently indicate the presence of a white dwarf companion, providing strong support for this scenario. Comparisons with FRUITY AGB nucleosynthesis models show that the residual neutron-capture abundance pattern is best reproduced by a low-mass AGB companion with an initial mass of approximately 3.0 $M_{\odot}$. Its enhancements of C, N, Na, and s-process elements make it chemically distinct from the other confirmed GD-1 members. These results identify J0930+2902 as a fossil record of binary mass transfer preserved in the ancient GD-1 stellar stream, demonstrating that binary interaction can leave long-lived chemical signatures in accreted stellar populations.

line racer: Rapid Calculation of Exoplanetary Radiative Opacities

David B. Hägele, Paul Mollière, Michiel Min

Submitted for review to the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS)

PDFThu 26 Nov
Detailed studies of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres rely on precise knowledge of the spectral features of possible atmospheric species. These features are a result of the interaction of different molecules and atoms with the radiation of the host star or the intrinsic thermal radiation of the object. The interaction is described by the opacity of a species, which determines how much light is absorbed at a given wavelength. The strength and shape of these opacities are very dependent on the temperature and pressure of the atmosphere, which is why they have to be calculated for a wide range of conditions. line racer is a Python package that enables computing high-resolution opacities from large molecular and atomic line lists in an effective manner. It offers users a wide range of options to customize opacity calculations to their needs and available hardware. The code is designed for efficient parallelization on multi-core and multi-node systems and can produce outputs compatible with popular atmospheric modeling and retrieval tools.

Beyond the blur: Radial binning trumps stellar migration in resolved star formation histories

Charlotte Olsen, Charlotte Welker, Ena Chia, Anna C Wright

29 pages, 19 figures, Submitted to ApJ

PDFThu 26 Nov
Spatially resolved galaxy properties are routinely derived from integral-field spectroscopy and increasingly from multi-band photometry as a wealth of photometric data become available in large surveys like LSST/Rubin. Spatially resolved star formation histories (SFHs) offer a detailed view of galaxy growth and quenching by tracing the timing and location of star formation within a galaxy up to one billion years in the past. However, stellar migration between spaxels may strongly bias these reconstructions. Quantifying this bias remains challenging as few Milky-Way mass simulations fully resolve initial stellar dispersions or migration rates. We use the well-validated h277 Milky-Way-mass cosmological zoom simulation, which resolves both via explicitly tying star formation to the non-equilibrium abundance of H2, to assess the quality of specific star formation rates (sSFR) radial profiles inferred from resolved SFHs against actual values from stellar particle tracking. Across several evolutionary windows spanning a range of stellar activity stages from quiescent to star-bursting, we find that the adaptive radial binning imposed by S/N constraints in photometric SED fitting actually mitigates most of the blurring/mixing effects of stellar migration on inferred radial profiles up to lookback times of 1.5 Gyr. This allows for proper recovery of not only the average sSFR but also its radial slope, its relative changes in scatter across radial annuli and even approximate localization of low-z star-forming clumps. Only galaxies having undergone a major merger across the considered lookback time display discrepant, unreliable sSFR profiles, hence should not be considered for such reconstructions.

An oxygen-rich supernova remnant in NGC 253 with narrow [N II] emission lines

Timo Kravtsov, Enrico Congiu, Joseph P. Anderson, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Seppo Mattila +10

6 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication in A&A

PDFThu 26 Nov
Context. Supernova remnants (SNRs) are the final evolutionary stage of supernovae. In rare cases, the remnant persists as an optically luminous remnant decades after the explosion. We report the discovery of an unusual oxygen-rich (O-rich) SNR that was serendipitously discovered in the MUSE mosaic of the nearby (D $\sim$ 3.5 Mpc) galaxy NGC 253 released by arXiv:2506.14921. Aims. We search for SNRs in MUSE integral field spectroscopy data of NGC 253. Methods. We search for unresolved point sources with broad and strong [O III]$\lambda$$\lambda$4959,5007, [O I]$\lambda$$\lambda$6300,6364 or [O II]$\lambda$$\lambda$7320,7331 emission lines. We also search for possible counterparts at other wavelengths in archival data. Results. We find a single O-rich SNR in NGC 253 with [O III]$\lambda$$\lambda$4959,5007. For this object, we report a coincident X-ray source detected by Chandra and a non-detection at mid-infrared wavelengths by JWST. Additionally, we identify [N II]$\lambda$$\lambda$6548,6583 emission lines and no detectable hydrogen or [SII]$\lambda$$\lambda$6716,6731 emission. The [N II] emission lines are broader (230 km/s) than the surrounding interstellar medium lines but still narrow in comparison to the [O III] emission (>1500 km/s) from the SNR. No detections of [O I]$\lambda$$\lambda$6300,6364 and [O II]$\lambda$$\lambda$7320,7331 were made. Conclusions. The discovery of a single O-rich SNR after a systematic search of NGC 253 highlights their scarcity in nearby galaxies. The structure of [O III] emission indicates complex structure in the O-rich ejecta. The relative narrowness of [N II] emission lines compared to the [O III] lines and the non-detection of hydrogen show that the remnant is surrounded by an N-rich circumstellar medium. The ejecta is currently interacting with this material of the preceding supernova explosion.

JWST Reveals Contrast Overdensities around Two ALMA-CRISTAL Galaxies at $z\sim5.2$

Shaoze Geng, Siwei Zou, Manuel Aravena, Nikolaus Z. Prusinski, Yi W. Ren +6

Submitted, comments are welcome

PDFThu 26 Nov
The distribution of stellar mass between massive galaxies and their companions traces how galaxy assembly proceeds within early large-scale structure. We investigate the environments of two galaxies from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) CRISTAL survey: CRISTAL-19 (C19; $z=5.235$) and CRISTAL-21 (C21; $z=5.256$), using F444W slitless spectroscopy from the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in COSMOS-3D. A friends-of-friends analysis of H$\alpha$ emitters identifies two distinct overdense nodes separated by approximately 25 comoving Mpc. Although C21 is the more massive galaxy, C19 has the more massive, actively star-forming companions. The companion populations around C19 and C21 have median stellar masses of $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)=9.43$ and 8.82 and median dust-corrected H$\alpha$ star formation rates of 31 and $16~M_\odot~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, respectively. Their star formation rate contrast largely reflects the difference in companion masses. C19 contains only $4.5^{+0.9}_{-0.7}\%$ of the combined measured stellar mass of itself and its selected companions; the corresponding fraction for C21 is $39^{+5}_{-5}\%$. Thus, stellar mass remains more widely distributed among galaxies around C19, whereas a larger share resides in C21. Resolved interacting companions around C19 and [C II] kinematics consistent with a late-stage merger in C21 support this contrast in assembly state. These findings support the phase-dependent picture of Zou et al. (2026), in which the surrounding star-forming population changes as interactions and mergers build up a massive galaxy.

Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU): the fraction of radio-detected quasi-stellar objects at high redshift

A. Caccianiga, D. Dallacasa, L. Ighina, A. Moretti, J. Afonso +10

Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics

PDFThu 26 Nov
The aim of this paper is to use the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) to assess the fraction of high-z quasi-stellar objects (QSOs) that are radio-emitting at ~0.2 mJy/beam level and to establish if the radio emission is mainly produced by relativistic jets. A sample of 808 type1 QSOs in the redshift range 4<z<9 and covering the sky area currently observed by EMU was compiled from the literature and the SDSS spectroscopic database and cross-matched with EMU source catalogue. In total, 124 high-z QSOs are detected by EMU, corresponding to 15% of the sample. The large majority (70%) of the QSOs radio detected by EMU are reported in the radio for the first time. We use this sample to establish the detection rate at different optical magnitudes. We show that the fraction of radio-loud (R>10) high-z QSOs is about 8% while the fraction of radio detections is a strong function of the optical magnitude and reaches values of ~35% when only the optically brightest (mag~18) QSOs are considered. Since all the radio detected QSOs, including those classified as radio-quiet (R<10), exhibit radio powers ranging from 5x10^24 to 5x10^27 W Hz^-1 at 5 GHz, we argue that they could all host a relativistic jet and that orientation could be one of the main causes of the different values of radio-loudness observed in the sample. To support this hypothesis, we show that the number of high-z QSOs detected by EMU is fully consistent with the predictions based on the beaming model, using as reference the high-z blazars discovered at higher radio flux densities. The results presented here suggest that relativistic jets could have been very common in the early Universe representing up to ~35% of the luminous (L_1450A>10^46 erg s^-1) QSO population. Future observations with SKAO will be instrumental to unambiguously confirm the jetted nature of the QSOs currently detected by EMU.

Superfit: A Supernova Spectral Classification Tool with Host-Galaxy Decomposition

D. Andrew Howell, Alyona Kosobokova, Samantha Goldwasser, Ido Irani, Saanvi Tiwary +2

Submitted to AJ, 11 pages, 8 figures

PDFThu 26 Nov
Superfit is a an open-source tool for automated spectroscopic classification of supernovae that accounts for redshift, reddening, and host-galaxy contamination. Here we present the latest version, which has been rewritten in Python and is now available as a web-based application. A user uploads an observed spectrum, and Superfit uses a curated library of transient and galaxy spectra to perform a simultaneous fit of transient and host galaxy spectra, while adjusting for color and redshift. In contrast to machine-learning algorithms, Superfit uses a least squares fitting approach, which is reproducible, verifiable, and understandable to users. The user may specify the binning of the spectra, set redshift and reddening limits, phase information, and restrict host galaxy and supernova templates for fitting. A new, expanded template library includes modern transient subclasses and associated observational metadata. A modern browser-based interface allows users to configure fitting parameters, visualize spectra, monitor fitting progress, and interactively inspect and compare ranked candidate matches and their individual components. We describe the fitting methodology, template library, software architecture, and web interface, and demonstrate its capabilities through classification examples.

AT2024dky as an Off-nuclear Tidal Disruption Event Candidate

Yuhan Yao, Ryan Chornock, Itai Sfaradi, Jinyi Shangguan, Raffaella Margutti +16
